title: THE BIBLE’S ANSWER TO FORBIDDEN SEX ISN’T HATING SEX—It Includes Delighting in Faithful Sex
paragraphs: THE BIBLE’S ANSWER TO FORBIDDEN SEX ISN’T HATING SEX—It Includes Delighting in Faithful Sex

God did not create sexual desire and then become embarrassed by it. The Bible’s answer to lust, adultery, pornography, fornication, and sexual betrayal is not the destruction of desire—but the redemption of desire under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
There is something the enemy desperately wants Christians to misunderstand about sex.
If he cannot convince you that every desire should be obeyed, he will try to convince you that every desire should be hated.
Either worship sex...
or become ashamed that sexuality exists at all.
Either make pleasure your god...
or quietly suspect that holiness means God would rather human beings never experience it.
But Scripture refuses both lies.
And buried in the middle of a biblical warning against sexual ruin is a sentence so passionate that some Christians might be surprised it is actually in the Bible.
The warning begins with forbidden desire.
Then suddenly Scripture says:
“Let your fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
And then it becomes even more intimate:
“Let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
That is Proverbs 5:18–19.
Read it again.
Not a romance novel.
Not modern sexual propaganda.
Scripture.
And the Hebrew makes the point even harder to escape.
The command translated “rejoice” comes from שָׂמַח — samach — language of gladness and rejoicing.
Then comes the startling expression traditionally rendered “be thou ravished always with her love.”
The Hebrew verb שָׁגָה — shagah — can carry the idea of being captivated, intoxicated, or swept away.
The same chapter that warns a man not to give himself to forbidden sexual desire tells him to become captivated by the love of his own wife.
That changes the conversation.
The Bible does not merely say...
“Do not commit adultery.”
It also says, in effect...
Delight in your spouse.
Do not merely run away from counterfeit intimacy.
Cultivate covenant intimacy.
Do not merely say no to what is forbidden.
Learn the holy beauty of saying yes to what God has given.
And perhaps that is exactly what somebody reading this needed to hear.
Because maybe your story with sexuality has been nothing but shame.
Maybe nobody ever taught you the difference between sexual desire and sexual sin.
Maybe your first education about sex came through pornography.
Maybe someone introduced you to things your young mind was never prepared to carry.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you promised God you would never cross.
Maybe you slept with someone because loneliness became louder than conviction.
Maybe you committed adultery.
Maybe adultery was committed against you.
Maybe you have deleted the browser history...
but not the memory.
Maybe you have repented ten times, fifty times, a hundred times, and somewhere underneath all those prayers is a terrifying question:
“Can Jesus really make someone clean after this?”
Listen carefully.
Yes.
Not because sexual sin does not matter.
Because the blood of Jesus does.
Christianity does not minimize sexual sin.
Christianity announces a Savior greater than sexual sin.
There is an enormous difference.
The Gospel does not say your body is meaningless.
It says your body matters so profoundly that Paul writes:
And then:
“Ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body.”
That is 1 Corinthians 6:19–20.
The Greek word repeatedly associated in the New Testament with sexual immorality is πορνεία — porneia.
Its biblical usage encompasses sexual immorality rather than merely an uncomfortable feeling of attraction.
That distinction matters.
Temptation is not permission.
Desire is not automatically obedience.
And having a body capable of sexual attraction does not make the body evil.
God created humanity embodied.
“Male and female created he them.”
Before Genesis ever describes humanity's fall, Genesis describes the first husband and wife becoming “one flesh.”
Before sin corrupted human sexuality...
God created human sexuality.
Sin is therefore not the inventor of sex.
Sin is the vandal.
And Jesus did not come to hand the vandal ownership of what God designed.
This is why biblical sexual ethics can sound restrictive until you understand what Scripture is protecting.
Fire in a fireplace can warm a home.
Fire consuming the curtains can destroy it.
The problem is not that fire exists.
The question is where it burns.
Sexual desire detached from covenant can become extraordinarily destructive because sexuality reaches far beyond skin.
Bodies remember.
Hearts attach.
Trust can be shattered.
Children can be affected.
Marriages can collapse.
People can become objects.
Pleasure can become addiction.
Secret fantasies can slowly train a person to consume human beings in imagination rather than love them as image-bearers.
And therefore God's boundaries are not evidence that He hates pleasure.
Sometimes the existence of a boundary proves the value of what is being protected.
You lock a vault because something precious is inside.
You put rails beside a mountain road because the view is beautiful and the cliff is real.
You teach a child not to touch a flame because warmth is good but fire is powerful.
And God places sexual intimacy within covenant because sexuality is powerful enough to create extraordinary closeness—and powerful enough to leave extraordinary wounds when treated carelessly.
That is why Hebrews 13:4 can hold celebration and warning together:
“Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.”
Notice what Christianity does not say.
Marriage is honorable...
and the marriage bed is not described as inherently dirty.
The problem is not marital intimacy.
The problem is the violation of God's design.
This is why Proverbs can warn against the forbidden woman while simultaneously telling the husband to rejoice in his wife.
It is why Scripture can condemn adultery without condemning attraction between husband and wife.
It is why the Song of Songs can contain extraordinarily tender—and sometimes startlingly physical—poetry between lovers.
Song of Songs 4:10 in Hebrew begins:
מַה־יָּפוּ דֹדַיִךְ
Mah-yafu dodayikh...
“How beautiful is your love...”
The Song does not portray covenantal love as sterile religious duty.
There is admiration.
Longing.
Beauty.
Desire.
Delight.
The Bible is far less embarrassed about married lovers delighting in one another than many Christians have sometimes been.
But here is where we must be equally careful.
Biblical permission for marital sexual delight must never become permission for selfishness, coercion, humiliation, manipulation, or abuse.
Sex inside marriage is not transformed into holiness merely because two people possess a marriage certificate.
Christlike love still matters.
Tenderness matters.
Faithfulness matters.
Mutuality matters.
Care matters.
Consent matters.
Your spouse is not an object provided by God to satisfy you.
Your spouse is a person made in the image of God whom you are commanded to love.

Paul's language in 1 Corinthians 7 is striking because marital responsibility runs in both directions. He addresses the husband's obligation toward his wife and the wife's toward her husband, and when temporary abstinence is discussed, Paul speaks explicitly of mutual agreement.
That was profoundly significant.
Biblical marital intimacy is not supposed to sound like:
“You owe me your body.”
Its trajectory is:
“I belong to you in covenant love, and I will not treat your body as something to exploit.”
Because Christian marriage is never ultimately about domination.
It is supposed to reflect sacrificial love.
And Ephesians points us toward the staggering model:
Christ and His Church.
Christ does not exploit His Bride.
He gives Himself for her.
He loves.
He sacrifices.
He sanctifies.
He remains faithful.
So when Christianity says “no” to adultery, pornography, fornication, exploitation, and sexual immorality, that “no” is standing beside an enormous “yes.”
Yes to faithfulness.
Yes to covenant.
Yes to tenderness.
Yes to husband and wife knowing one another without hiding.
Yes to desire that does not require betrayal.
Yes to pleasure without the morning-after terror of wondering whose life was just shattered.
Yes to intimacy that can look another person in the eyes without needing secrecy to survive.
Yes to a marriage bed that Hebrews can call undefiled.
And ultimately...
yes to Jesus becoming Lord even over our sexuality.
Because this is where Christianity becomes uncomfortable for every one of us.
Jesus does not merely want your Sunday morning.
He wants your body.
Your imagination.
Your browser history.
Your dating life.
Your marriage.
Your private messages.
Your fantasies.
Your loneliness.
Your wounds.
Your desires.
Your secret compromises.
The parts of yourself you proudly display...
and the parts you desperately password-protect.
You cannot meaningfully say, “Jesus is Lord,” while deliberately constructing rooms in your life where Jesus is forbidden to enter.
And maybe that sentence just found one of those rooms.
Maybe nobody knows what happens after midnight.
Maybe your spouse thinks everything is fine.
Maybe your church friends would never imagine what is hidden behind your screen.
Maybe you know exactly which app you keep reinstalling.
Maybe there is somebody else's husband...
somebody else's wife...
someone you are sleeping with but have never covenanted your life to...
a secret conversation you keep telling yourself is “only friendship”...
a pornography habit you have renamed “stress relief”...
a fantasy life you protect because surrender feels too painful.
You do not need another clever excuse.
You need Jesus.
Not merely Jesus as religious decoration.
Jesus as Savior.
Jesus as Lord.
Jesus in the locked room.
Jesus beside the hidden browser.
Jesus inside the loneliness.
Jesus standing before the shame you thought disqualified you forever.
And here is the part scandal never expects:
Grace.
Real grace.
Not cheap grace that calls darkness light.
Grace that enters darkness and turns on the light.
When the woman caught in adultery was dragged before Jesus, her sin was not imaginary.
Her humiliation was public.
Her scandal had become entertainment for religious men.
Yet after her accusers disappeared, Christ did not crush her.
Neither did He redefine adultery into righteousness.
Grace and truth stood together.
“Neither do I condemn thee.”
And then:
“Go, and sin no more.”
That is Jesus.
No condemnation used as permission to remain enslaved.
No holiness preached without mercy for the broken.
Grace does not say sin never mattered.
Grace says sin will not get the final word when a sinner comes to Christ.
Maybe your sexual history has chapters you wish you could tear out.
Christ knows every page.
And He still calls sinners to Himself.
The Cross is where our excuses die...
and where condemned sinners discover mercy.
Christ “bare our sins in his own body on the tree.”
He did not bleed because sin was trivial.
He bled because redemption was costly.
And when a sinner turns to Him in repentance and faith, Scripture does not describe that person as permanently contaminated merchandise.
Paul once listed devastating sins in 1 Corinthians 6, including sexual sins.
Then came three of the most beautiful words imaginable:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Past tense.
Then:
“but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus.”
Do you understand?
Your worst sexual failure does not have to become your permanent name.
Adulterer does not have to be your final name.
Porn addict does not have to be your final name.
Fornicator does not have to be your final name.
Unclean does not have to be your final name.
Your scandal may explain something about your history.
It does not possess authority to write your ending.
Jesus does.
But grace invites surrender.
If you are living in sexual sin, repentance is not feeling terrible while arranging to repeat it tomorrow.
Repentance turns.
It may mean ending the affair.
Deleting the secret account.
Confessing what needs to be brought into light.
Seeking mature pastoral accountability.
Installing real boundaries.
Leaving the situation that continually feeds temptation.
Getting wise Christian counseling where deep wounds, compulsive behavior, betrayal, or abuse are involved.
It may hurt.
Freedom sometimes begins with an incision.
But whatever obedience costs you, slavery eventually charges more.
And for married couples reading this...
perhaps your challenge is different.

Maybe you have spent years hearing what Christians are forbidden to do sexually but almost nothing about cultivating affection, tenderness, romance, playfulness, patience, communication, and delight inside marriage.
Maybe your marriage has become efficient but cold.
Bills are paid.
Children are transported.
Meals happen.
Schedules synchronize.
You sleep inches apart...
and somehow live miles away.
Come closer.
Talk.
Listen.
Court each other again.
Pray together.
Forgive.
Learn tenderness again.
Do not allow pornography to educate your expectations.
Do not compare the person you covenanted with to edited bodies, manufactured fantasies, or fictional performances.
Look at the person God entrusted to you.
See a soul.
See an image-bearer.
See the years you have survived together.
See the sacrifices nobody else witnessed.
And rediscover the biblical possibility of delight.
“Rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
Not tolerate.
Not merely coexist.
Rejoice.
There are marriages that do not need another lecture about forbidden sex nearly as much as they need permission to recover faithful affection.
There are spouses starving for tenderness while sleeping beside someone who thinks fidelity merely means never committing adultery.
Faithfulness is more beautiful than simply refusing to betray.
Faithfulness learns to cherish.
And to the unmarried Christian, holiness is not God sentencing you to worthlessness until somebody puts a ring on your finger.
Jesus Himself was never married.
Your human worth is therefore not measured by sexual experience, romantic attention, or marital status.
Chastity is not the absence of personhood.
Singleness is not spiritual inferiority.
Your deepest identity is not “desired” or “undesired” by another human being.
If you belong to Christ, your life belongs to Christ.
And whether married or single, every Christian ultimately brings sexuality beneath the same throne.
Jesus is Lord.
That is the Bible's answer.
Not:
“Sex is god.”
Not:
“Sex is disgusting.”
But:
God is God.
And therefore His gifts are enjoyed rightly when His gifts remain beneath His lordship.
That is freedom.
Not having permission to obey every appetite.
Freedom is reaching the point where appetite no longer owns you.
Somebody reading this is exhausted from being owned.
If that is you, stop hiding.
Not from us.
From Christ.
Tonight, get honest before God.
No performance.
No Christian vocabulary designed to make rebellion sound respectable.
Tell Him the truth.
Bring the filth.
Bring the loneliness.
Bring the memories.
Bring the appetite.
Bring the betrayal.
Bring the wounds somebody else caused.
Bring what you chose.
Bring what was done to you.
Bring the confusion.
Bring all of it to Jesus.

And remember carefully: if sexual violence, coercion, exploitation, or abuse was committed against you, another person's sin against you is not your moral guilt. Seek safety and trustworthy help. Christ's compassion for the wounded should never be twisted into protection for an abuser.
But where you have sinned...
repent.
Where you have been wounded...
seek healing.
Where you have betrayed...
tell the truth and pursue restoration without demanding that wounded people heal according to your timetable.
Where you have become enslaved...
bring the chains into the light.
Where your marriage has become cold...
begin rebuilding tenderness.
Where desire has become your master...
put it beneath Christ.
And where shame keeps whispering, “Jesus could never want someone with your history”...
look at the Cross.
The Gospel has always been God's answer to people with histories.
Be honest.

And if you have experienced Christ bringing you out of sexual bondage, shame, betrayal, or destructive relationships, consider sharing your testimony without exposing private details that belong to someone else. Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that repentance is possible and grace is real.
Not because sharing makes you righteous.
Because somebody you know may be drowning quietly.
Send this privately to the friend who has been fighting alone.
Not as a purchase of God's favor.
Not as a way to buy a blessing.
Not as a substitute for obedience.
Give first where God has convicted you to give, support the faithful work of your local church, care for people in need, and practice generosity with a willing heart.
If you want to glorify God through your resources, ask Him where He wants you to give.
Gospel ministry has always been carried forward not only by those who preach and teach, but also by believers who pray, share, give, encourage, and help send the message farther.

If this ministry has strengthened you, challenged you, helped you return to Scripture, or put Christ before your eyes during a difficult season, you can become part of sustaining and expanding that mission here:
Pray whether or not you can give.
Because the goal was never to build consumers around Gospel Warrior.
The goal is to point sinners, wounded people, marriages, families, prodigals, seekers, and exhausted believers toward Jesus Christ.
The world has preached about sex loudly.
Pornography has preached.
Hollywood has preached.
Hookup culture has preached.
Shame has preached.
Religious hypocrisy has preached.
Your wounds may have preached.
Your appetites may have preached.
Your regrets certainly know how to preach.
But none of them gets the final sermon.
Jesus does.
And His message to the sexually broken is neither “Your sin does not matter” nor “Your life is over.”
It is something infinitely more powerful.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Receive mercy.
Learn holiness.
Discover that God's boundaries are not the graveyard of joy.
And find out that the Savior who forgives sinners can teach redeemed people how to desire differently, love faithfully, live honestly, and walk free.
Your scandal may be written in ink across yesterday.
But grace is already holding the pen over tomorrow.
